Letter of May 17, 1972, to the State Clearinghouse from Director, 3ffice of Planning and Program Development, Washington Department of Ecology.
This letter points out that "Resolution of the problems Comment: encountered by endangered species should include the adequate consideration of all components of ecosystems within which the endangered animal exists." We acknowledge that the ultimate program for preserving endangered species must eventually consider protection of ecosystems. A program for protection of endangered ecosystems would include preservation of endangered species of plants and animals as well. However, because of the degree to which some ecosystems have changed -- change in which only some of the components of that original ecosystem have survived -- certain species cannot be preserved within the context of their original ecosystem. Within ecosystems that still remain intact, successful protection of any member of that ecosystem will also favor survival of the entire ecosystem. It is possible that though an ecosystem may be endangered, none of its components may be threatened in the same sense. The object of preservation is a particular association of species. While we agree with Washington that the ultimate endangered species program should include preservation of ecosystems, we cannot postpone species preservation until ecosystems are recognized by encompassing legislation. Individual species recovery programs under the proposed legislation will most certainly include protection of the ecosystem of which that species is a part.
